name: Fluting and reeding
summary: Parallel grooves (flutes) or ridges (reeds) on a column, a panel, a leg or a sheet of glass.
how: Cut 16 to 24 flutes round a column, or set the grooves at 15 to 40mm centres on a flat panel.
Run the flutes vertical to make a surface look taller.
Use one fluted surface in each room as an accent.

origin.note: Greek Doric and Ionic columns carry vertical concave grooves; a Doric shaft has 20 flutes.

adoptions.via: Jacques-Germain Soufflot gives the Pantheon in Paris, begun in 1764, a portico of fluted Corinthian columns.
Wedgwood and Boulton copy classical urns and columns, and the cabinet makers of the pattern books turn flutes on slim mahogany legs.
Neoclassical and Regency furniture takes fluted and reeded legs and friezes.
Art Deco rooms use fluted pilasters, fluted glass and fluted wood panels.
Reeded glass and fluted wood or stone cover cabinets, islands and walls.

sources.title: John Summerson, The Classical Language of Architecture (1963)
